title: The Queenship of Mary (22 August)
hook: a week after the Assumption, Mary honored as queen

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen of Hungary, the king remembered for his admonitions and his crown. Your line was the holy crown. What did you hold with care yesterday? Day one thousand seventeen.

A week ago the Church kept the Assumption: Mary, taken body and soul into heaven. Today the story takes one more step. In the rosary, right after the Assumption, comes the last glorious mystery, and it's a coronation. It turns up in paintings and stained glass: gold, stars, and a crown lowered onto Mary's head by her Son. Yesterday's crown sat on a king. Today's sits on a woman from a small town who married a carpenter. That raises a fair question. Why call her a queen at all? And what kind of queen would she be? Today's feast answers with two words that belong together. The Queenship of Mary.
screen: `A WEEK AFTER THE ASSUMPTION.` → `THE LAST GLORIOUS MYSTERY.` → `WHY A QUEEN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Gospel, because the title begins there. Before Jesus is born, the angel tells Mary what kind of son he will be. In the Douay-Rheims: "and of his kingdom there shall be no end." A king. Catholics reason from that in one short step: the mother of the king is the queen. When Mary arrives at her cousin's house, Elizabeth greets her: "whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Mother of my Lord. Second, the old kingdom of Israel. In the story of Solomon, David's son, the king's mother is given a seat of honor. When Bathsheba comes to her son Solomon, he rises to meet her and has a throne set for the king's mother, "and she sat on his right hand." And notice why she came: to ask a favor for someone else. Catholics read Mary in that seat. Not ruling in her Son's place, but near him, bringing other people's requests. Third, the last book of the Bible, the Apocalypse: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." Readers have heard Israel in that woman, or the Church; Catholic tradition also hears Mary. Fourth, what kind of queen. Catholic teaching is careful here. Mary is not a goddess. She is a creature, like everyone else, honored because of her Son. Her crown is a mother's crown. That's why the old hymn, the Salve Regina, greets her as queen and, in the same breath, as mother of mercy. The two titles explain each other. Other Christians honor Mary in other ways, and some don't use this title at all.
screen: `OF HIS KINGDOM, NO END.` · `THE KING'S MOTHER AT HIS RIGHT HAND.` · `A CROWN OF TWELVE STARS.` · `A MOTHER'S CROWN, NOT A GODDESS.` · then, large: `QUEEN AND MOTHER OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the Salve Regina. Settle, and breathe. If you pray and you know it, pray it slowly, from its opening words, Hail, holy Queen, all the way through, with a breath between the lines. If you don't know it, hold its first two titles side by side for the sit. Queen. Mother. Notice which one feels far away and which one feels close. If you don't pray, bring to mind someone who has authority over you and still treats you like family. Hold them in mind with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Salve Regina, the old hymn greeting Mary as queen. The Queenship of Mary is the feast, a week after the Assumption, that honors her as queen because she is the mother of the King.
Your line: queen and mother. Today, if you have someone's ear, use it once to ask a favor for someone else, not for yourself. Day one thousand seventeen.

howItsDone: On 22 August Catholics keep the memorial of the Queenship of Mary; Catholics pray the Salve Regina, one of the Marian antiphons that can close Night Prayer, and the last glorious mystery of the rosary is her coronation.

notes: Claims rule: no founding date for the feast is given (Pius XII, Ad Caeli Reginam, 1954; moved to 22 August in the 1969 calendar). Confirm it is fine to leave out.

The Bathsheba / queen-mother (gebirah) reading is a common Catholic argument; the script notes she came to ask for someone else (Adonijah), but does not mention that Solomon refused her. Confirm the framing is fair.
Practice cites the Salve Regina only by its opening words in English ('Hail, holy Queen'); confirm the traditional English wording is acceptable to quote this briefly.
howItsDone: confirm the Salve Regina's place at the end of Compline for part of the year (from Trinity Sunday to Advent in the current Liturgy of the Hours).
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:33, Luke 1:43, 3 Kings 2:19 and Apocalypse 12:1.

Audit: carry still modeled the listener on Bathsheba's request (which Solomon refused and which led to Adonijah's death); reworded to stand on its own. 'Some hear the Church, and Catholics also hear Mary' implied Catholics don't read it as the Church; reworded.

Editor: 'In David's line, the king's mother had a seat of honor' narrowed to what 3 Kings 2:19 says (Solomon's mother given a seat); carry reworded so it no longer leans on Bathsheba's refused request; howItsDone softened on Night Prayer and matched to the hook's 'last glorious mystery'.
